Shared Python<->Rust parity corpus for PATH ANCESTRY.
Python home:  vco_lib/project_move.py::path_compare_key / _parts / is_ancestor
Rust  mirror: launcher/src-tauri/vct-launcher-core/src/db/bindings_writer.rs
::path_parts / is_ancestor
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS (v0.2.92 MAJOR-12). bindings_writer.rs carried a
'MUST MATCH vco_lib/project_move.py' tier-C mirror comment that named
tests/test_v0292_wp18_rename_delivery.py as the thing bounding the
divergence risk, 'driving the SAME fixture table through both
implementations'. No such table existed: that file asserted only that the
strings 'fn is_ancestor' and 'MUST MATCH' appeared in the Rust source --
both satisfiable by a comment -- and path_compare_key had zero test hits
repo-wide. Underneath the false claim the two implementations really did
disagree: is_ancestor('/a', '/a/b/../..') was False in Python and True in
Rust. This file is the table the comment always claimed.
THE '..' DECISION. Both sides now COLLAPSE '.' and '..' lexically, i.e.
Python's os.path.normpath / ntpath.normpath behaviour won and the Rust
mirror adopted it. Three reasons, in order:
1. The mirror follows its home. bindings_writer.rs itself names
project_move.py as 'the tested Python home for this rule'.
2. The consumer REWRITES user data. repoint_kg_dir_path re-points a
user-owned kg_dir_path column for every row it judges to be under the
old root. Collapsing '..' yields FEWER ancestor matches, so the
not-collapsing behaviour was a false-POSITIVE write: it rewrote a row
whose stored path lexically resolves to '/' and is not under the root
at all. CLAUDE.md's conservative-defaults rule settles that direction.
3. Adopting the Rust behaviour in Python would have opened a second
hole: paths_equal('/a', '/a/b/..') would become False, so the move
preflight's overlap guard would stop recognising a destination that
is lexically the source.
Lexical collapsing can disagree with a symlinked reality ('/a/link/..' is
not necessarily '/a'). That is accepted and deliberate: path_compare_key
documents that it must NOT touch the filesystem, and callers that need a
resolved path resolve first (_resolve_for_compare).
SHAPES. Rust has ONE function used on three OSes; Python has three shapes.
Each vector declares which:
posix-sensitive   -> Python platform='linux',  Rust case_insensitive=false
posix-insensitive -> Python platform='darwin', Rust case_insensitive=true
windows           -> Python platform='win32',  Rust case_insensitive=true
WHAT THIS CORPUS DOES NOT PIN, and why -- read before adding vectors:
* Unicode case folding. Python casefolds (full folding: 'STRASSE' vs
'strasse'), Rust str::to_lowercase does simple lowercasing. They
disagree on inputs like 'ß'. Closing that needs a full-folding crate in
the launcher, which is out of proportion to a path component; the
corpus therefore stays ASCII on the case axis and the divergence is
recorded here rather than hidden.
* A literal backslash used as a FILENAME character on POSIX. Rust's
path_parts always splits on both separators; Python's posix shapes
treat '\\' as an ordinary character. So a directory genuinely named
'a\\b' on Linux is one component to Python and two to Rust. Closing it
needs a separator flag threaded through repoint_kg_dir_path_ci's public
signature (case-insensitivity alone cannot express it: macOS is
case-insensitive with POSIX separators). Posix-shape vectors below
therefore use '/' only.
* Windows drive-RELATIVE paths ('C:a', meaning 'a, relative to the CWD
on drive C'). The launcher stores absolute paths; ntpath models the
per-drive CWD and the Rust mirror does not.
Both sides assert against this file, so a one-sided edit fails on BOTH:
Python via tests/test_v0292_wp18_rename_delivery.py::TestPathAncestryParity,
Rust via bindings_writer.rs::path_ancestry_matches_shared_fixture. An
unreadable or unparsable fixture is a hard failure on both sides, never a
skip -- a skip would reintroduce exactly the silence this file closes.
